title: The Pilgrims and the Puritans
hookLine: crossing the Atlantic for religious freedom; their story with Native peoples is honestly mixed

lines: EXILES WHO WANTED TO WORSHIP FREELY.
cards: A small, crowded ship called the Mayflower drops anchor off a cold coast in late autumn.
At the heart of the group on board are English Christians who wanted to worship their own way, without the Church of England telling them how. Many have already lived as exiles in Holland.
Others on the ship came for land and work. The version told in school pageants ends with a shared harvest feast.
The real story is longer and harder, and it belongs just as much to the people already standing on that shore.

teach.b: First, two names that get mixed up. The Pilgrims were Separatists: they believed the Church of England was beyond fixing, so they left it.
The Puritans, who came after them and settled around Boston, wanted to stay in the church and purify it from within. Both crossed the Atlantic for the freedom to worship as they believed God wanted.
The Puritans' leader John Winthrop told his settlers they would be like a city upon a hill, with every eye on them.

He was reaching for Jesus' words in the Sermon on the Mount: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid." Now the people on the shore. The land around Plymouth was home to the Wampanoag.

The Pilgrims' own governor, William Bradford, wrote that after a hard first winter, an English-speaking Native man named Squanto came to help, showing them how to plant corn and where to fish, and that a peace was agreed with the Wampanoag leader Massasoit.
Bradford also wrote that Squanto had learned English after being carried off from his home. That peace held for a time. Later generations broke it, in land taken and in war.

And the Puritans who came for freedom punished or banished some who worshipped differently, as tomorrow's story shows. So the story is honestly mixed: real faith, real courage, real help received, and real harm done.
Which is why today's line is a question.

how: Congregational and other churches in New England trace their roots to the Pilgrims and Puritans, and some now hold services of remembrance and reconciliation with Wampanoag and other Native communities.

games.q: you're a Wampanoag leader. a ship of English settlers has come through a hard winter on your coast, and they're struggling. what do you do?
games.why: Bradford records that Massasoit made a peace with the settlers, and that Squanto helped them plant corn and fish. later generations broke that peace.

practice: Wherever you're sitting, people lived on this ground before the town around you had its name. Feel the floor, and the earth beneath it, and bring to mind the people who walked here first, whose names you may not know yet.
If you pray, remember them before God; if you don't, hold them in respectful attention.

wordCard.voice: Mayflower. The ship that carried the Pilgrims across the Atlantic to a shore already home to the Wampanoag, in a story of real help and real harm.

carryVoice: Your line: freedom for whom? A question worth keeping open. Day eight hundred eighty-five, done.
